question: Which body is the only one authorised to register real property rights in Dubai?
explanation: Law No. (7) of 2006 makes the Land Department the only body that registers real property rights and long-term leases. RERA regulates brokerages and similar activities but does not keep the Property Register.

question: A sale of a Dubai unit is signed but never entered in the Property Register. What is its legal position?
optionA: It is valid between the parties
optionD: It is valid once the fee is paid
explanation: Article 9 says a disposition that creates, transfers, varies or ends a real property right is not deemed valid unless it is recorded in the register.

question: Outside designated areas, who can hold full ownership of Dubai real property under Law No. (7) of 2006?
explanation: Article 4 limits full ownership to UAE nationals, GCC nationals and companies wholly owned by them or public joint stock companies. Others need the Ruler's approval or a designated area.

question: What is the longest leasehold or usufruct term a non-UAE national may be granted in a designated area?
explanation: Article 4 of Law No. (7) of 2006 and Regulation No. (3) of 2006 allow usufruct or leasehold rights of up to 99 years in the listed areas.

question: How can an entry in the Property Register be challenged?
explanation: Article 7 gives the register conclusive evidentiary value against everyone, open to challenge only on proof of fraud or forgery.

question: Where are the original registration documents and court rulings kept?
explanation: Article 5 says the originals stay with the Department and cannot be removed. Interested parties may inspect them and obtain certified copies.

question: Which task does Law No. (7) of 2006 give the Department besides keeping the register?
explanation: Article 6 lists the Department's duties, including preparing contract templates, setting rules for valuation and voluntary auctions, and keeping the real estate brokers register.

question: An heir wants to dispose of inherited property rights. What must be registered first?
optionA: A power of attorney from heirs
optionB: A tenancy contract for the unit
optionC: A valuation report on the estate
explanation: Article 11 requires the inheritance certificate to be registered. Until then the heir's disposal has no effect against third parties.

question: How does the Property Register treat an apartment building?
optionA: As one unit with supplementary owner records
optionB: As separate units, one entry for each floor
optionC: As common areas with no owner records
optionD: As unregistered until every unit is sold
explanation: Article 23 treats a multi-storey building as a single unit with one register entry, and supplementary records identify the owners of each apartment, floor and common area.

question: A deal is structured so that it gets around the registration rules. What is its status under Law No. (7) of 2006?
explanation: Article 26 voids any agreement or disposal that breaches the law, including those meant to get around it. The Department, the prosecution or the court can raise the invalidity.

question: A person has long possessed land that is not registered in his name. What may the Department do?
optionA: Transfer the plot to the government
optionB: Cancel the plot and its boundaries
optionC: Accept an application to regularise it
optionD: Order a forced sale of the land
explanation: Article 12 lets the Department accept applications from possessors of unregistered land to regularise their position, under procedures set by the Chairman.

question: Which duty does Law No. (7) of 2013 give the Land Department?
optionA: Setting bank lending rates for buyers
explanation: Article 6 includes preparing real property training programmes to qualify developers, real estate brokers and others working in the market.

question: Law No. (16) of 2007 created RERA. To which body is RERA affiliated?
explanation: Article 3 makes RERA a public corporation with its own legal personality, affiliated to the Land Department.

question: Which function did Law No. (16) of 2007 transfer from the Department to RERA?
explanation: Article 8 transferred the regulation of real estate brokerages and brokers, real estate studies, escrow account management and the supervision of Owners Associations.

question: Which of these is a stated objective of RERA?
optionD: Setting the price of off-plan units
explanation: Article 5 gives RERA the job of monitoring real estate advertisements in all media, along with licensing brokerages, accrediting escrow institutions and supervising Owners Associations.

question: Under Regulation No. (3) of 2006, where may non-UAE nationals acquire freehold ownership?
optionA: In any area after five years
explanation: Article 3 allows freehold, usufruct or leasehold rights only over the plots listed against each named area on the Department's maps.

question: The Department finds an obvious material error in the register. What may it do?
optionA: Correct it after notifying the parties
optionB: Wait for a court order to amend it
optionC: Delete the entry from the register
optionD: Leave it until the next sale
explanation: Article 13 allows the Department to correct obvious material errors, on application or on its own initiative, after notifying the concerned parties.

question: An owner merges two registered units. What must happen?
optionA: Only the plot map needs updating
optionB: The merger is recorded in the register
optionC: Both titles stay on separate records
optionD: The broker re-registers each of the units
explanation: Article 21 requires any division or merger of units to be recorded in the register.

question: Two units merge and only one carries a mortgage. What happens to the mortgage?
optionA: It lapses when the units merge
optionB: It covers only the original unit
optionC: It extends over the whole merged unit
optionD: It must be re-signed with a new lender
explanation: Under Article 20, where only one unit is encumbered the right extends to the whole merged unit without the beneficiary's approval.

question: A seller fails to honour his undertaking to transfer a property right. What is his liability limited to?
optionB: Loss of the plot to the buyer
optionC: Double the price paid so far
explanation: Article 10 limits liability for failing to honour such an undertaking to paying compensation, whether or not the agreement provides for it.

question: Under Bylaw No. (85) of 2006, who may carry on real estate brokerage in Dubai?
optionA: A person licensed and entered in the register
optionB: Any person holding a valid Emirates ID card
optionC: Any owner who sells a property himself
optionD: Any bank employee who handles mortgages
explanation: Article 3 bars anyone from brokerage activity unless licensed by the competent entities and entered in the Real Estate Brokers Register.

question: How many categories of real estate broker does Bylaw No. (85) of 2006 define?
explanation: Article 5 defines Category A (experienced brokers on the Roll, certified by the Chairman) and Category B (brokers practising under a licence from the competent entities).

question: Which broker category is exempt from the registration requirements of Chapter Two?
explanation: Category A brokers are on the Roll, certified by the Chairman and not licensed by the competent entities, so they are exempted from registration requirements.

question: Who approves or rejects a broker's registration application?
optionC: The Chairman of the Department alone
explanation: Article 10 gives the Committee the right to approve or reject applications. The Division only reviews and refers them.

question: Which membership certificate must a Category B application include?
optionA: Dubai Chamber of Commerce and Industry
explanation: Article 6(2) requires a certificate of membership in the Dubai Chamber of Commerce and Industry, alongside the trade licence.

question: What must an applicant show about the brokerage office premises?
optionA: A bank guarantee from a local bank
optionB: A title deed or tenancy contract
optionD: A utility bill for the office space
explanation: Article 6(4) asks for a true copy of the title deed of the office or a tenancy contract.

question: Which fact about the directors of a brokerage company blocks registration?
optionA: A past dispute with a tenant
optionD: An unpaid parking fine in the past
explanation: Article 6(6) requires that none of the directors or managers has been declared bankrupt or convicted of a crime affecting honour or trustworthiness.

question: Within what time must the Division refer a complete registration application to the Committee?
explanation: Article 9 requires referral within seven working days of submission or of receiving the missing documents.

question: When the Committee rejects a registration application, what must its decision contain?
explanation: Article 10 says any decision to reject an application for registration must be reasoned, and it is communicated to the applicant.

question: After a rejection, within how long from notification may the applicant re-apply once all requirements are met?
explanation: Article 11 lets the applicant re-apply upon fulfilling all requirements within fourteen days of being notified of the rejection.

question: Which details appear on the real estate broker card?
optionA: Name and bank account number held
optionB: Name and fees paid on registration
optionD: Name and rent paid for the office
explanation: Article 12 says the card bears the broker's name, address and registration number in the register.

question: Where must the broker's name and registration number appear?
optionA: Only on the card he carries
optionB: Only on the sale contracts he signs
optionC: Only in the entry in the register
explanation: Article 12 requires the name and registration number to appear in all correspondence and reports the broker issues.

question: Under Bylaw No. (85) of 2006, how often must a registered broker renew registration?
explanation: Article 13 requires a yearly renewal application on the relevant form.

question: When must a renewal application be filed?
optionA: On the day the certificate expires
optionC: Within 30 days after the expiry date
explanation: Article 13 requires the application at least thirty days before the registration certificate expires.

question: Which is the most severe penalty the Committee may impose under Article 39?
explanation: Article 39 lists a notice, a warning, suspension of activities for up to six months and blacklisting, in rising order of severity.

question: What is the longest suspension of activities the Committee may impose on a broker?
explanation: Article 39(3) allows suspension of activities for up to six months.

question: How many black points lead to cancellation of a broker's registration?
explanation: Article 40 cancels registration for breaching the code of ethics, a gross violation of the laws or accumulating three black points.

question: How long does a broker have to file a grievance against a cancellation decision?
explanation: Article 40 gives the broker fifteen days from notification to file a grievance with the Chairman.

question: Who decides a broker's grievance against cancellation?
optionA: The Committee, which can review it
optionB: Dubai Courts, on a fresh claim
optionC: The Chairman, whose ruling is final
explanation: Article 40 makes the Chairman's decision on the grievance final.

question: A registered broker suspends business for more than 12 successive months without an acceptable reason. What follows?
optionA: He receives a written warning only
optionB: His card is renewed for free
optionC: He moves into Category A status
explanation: Article 41 cancels registration where the broker suspends his business for more than twelve successive months without a reason the Committee accepts.

question: Which of these causes a broker to lose his status under Article 41?
optionB: Moving to another office in the area
optionC: Taking on a second licensed broker
explanation: Article 41(4) cancels registration proven to have been granted on false information given to the Division.

question: According to the RERA practice guide, what must exist before a broker card application is made in Trakheesi?
optionA: A marketing permit for the project
optionC: A Contract F signed with a buyer
optionD: An escrow account for the project
explanation: The guide says a real estate licence must first be obtained from the licensing authorities and registered in Trakheesi before the broker card application is submitted.

question: How is the validity of a real estate broker card linked on the Dubai Land Department's card service?
optionA: To the broker's Emirates ID expiry
optionB: To the passport of the owner
optionC: To the validity of the trade licence
optionD: To the length of the office lease
explanation: The card service states that the validity of the card is linked to the validity of the trade licence.

question: Which police document does a broker card application need?
optionC: A tax clearance certificate from the FTA
optionD: A Dubai Police good conduct certificate
explanation: The card service lists a personal photo, a copy of the Emirates ID and a good conduct certificate from the Dubai Police.

question: Where must a broker record every transaction he conducts?
explanation: Article 15 requires the broker to record all his transactions in his private register and to keep all the related documents.

question: A party to a deal asks the broker for the documents on it. What must the broker give?
explanation: Article 15 requires the broker to deliver a true copy of the documentation to the contracting parties on request.

question: For an off-plan sale by model, how long must the broker keep the plan or model?
optionA: For one year after the viewing
optionB: Until the unit is handed over
optionD: Until the next card renewal falls due
explanation: Article 15 says that in an off-plan sale or sale according to a model the broker keeps the plan or model until the transaction is concluded.

question: The Department asks a broker for statistics on his brokerage activity. What must he do?
explanation: Article 16 requires the broker to provide all information, data and statistics relating to the activity as the Department requests.

question: Which duty does a broker owe to his own client under Article 17?
optionB: Disclosing only the final agreed price
optionD: Sharing his fee split with rivals
explanation: Article 17 requires disclosure of all negotiation details and stages of the process so the client can decide whether to contract.

question: What must a broker tell the other contracting party?
optionA: His client's top price in the talks
optionD: Nothing, since he works for one side
explanation: Article 17 also requires disclosure to the other party of all substantial matters about the subject matter that are needed to avoid uncertainty.

question: A client insists on a transaction that breaks Dubai law. May the broker facilitate it?
explanation: Article 18 forbids facilitating any transaction that violates the laws or regulations in force in the Emirate.

question: A broker represents only the seller, but hides a defect he knows about and the buyer suffers. Is he answerable?
optionA: No, because he acts for the seller only
optionB: Only if the buyer is a resident
optionC: Only if he was paid a fee for it
optionD: Yes, for fraud or mistake he commits
explanation: Article 19 says that although he represents one party he must faithfully disclose the details he knows, and he is responsible for fraud or mistake.

question: The seller authorises a broker to act as the buyer in the deal he arranged. What happens to his remuneration?
optionA: He is not entitled to any
optionB: He receives half of the fee
optionD: The buyer pays him a flat sum
explanation: Article 20 allows this only if one party authorises it, and then the broker is not entitled to any remuneration.

question: A buyer gives a broker a cheque to hand to the seller. What is the broker's legal position?
explanation: Article 21 deems the broker the trustee of money or items delivered for safekeeping or for delivery to the other party, bound by the trusteeship rules.

question: A buyer's deposit is handed to a broker for safekeeping. What must he do with it?
explanation: As trustee under Article 21, the broker must deliver money or items as agreed by the parties.

question: When is a broker liable for losses suffered by the contracting parties?
optionA: Only when the whole contract fails
optionB: Never, since clients carry the risk
optionC: Only when he has received commission
optionD: When caused by his fraud or rule breach
explanation: Article 22 makes the broker liable for loss from his fraudulent act or deceit or from failing to observe the Bylaw or the code of professional ethics.

question: A broker accepts a promised benefit from the other party, against good faith. What happens to his fee?
optionA: He forfeits it and any expense refund
optionB: It is halved and the rest is held
optionC: It is taxed but still paid in full
optionD: It is unaffected if he discloses later
explanation: Article 23 makes the broker lose his right to remuneration and to a refund of expenses if he acts in the other party's interest or accepts such a promise.

question: Several brokers are engaged on one contract and nothing says they act separately. Their liability is:
explanation: Article 24 makes brokers engaged on one contract jointly liable unless they were authorised to work severally.

question: Several persons engage one broker for the same deal. Unless agreed otherwise, they are:
explanation: Article 25 holds them jointly responsible for implementing the engagement unless otherwise agreed.

question: Which of these is on the RERA practice guide's list of professional ethics?
explanation: The guide's ten ethics include fair treatment, respect, privacy, honesty, quality control, integrity, commitment to society, the interests of both parties, preserving documents and respecting Land Department procedures.

question: A broker uses a client's personal details for an unrelated promotion. Which ethic does this breach first?
explanation: Maintaining privacy is one of the ethics listed in the RERA practice guide, and personal data is not for unrelated use.

question: A broker quotes a buyer a larger floor area than the title deed shows. Which ethic does it breach first?
explanation: Honesty and uprightness is on the RERA guide's list of ethics, and the bylaw also makes the broker responsible for fraud or mistake.

question: A deal is concluded. What does the RERA guide's ethics list expect the broker to do with the deal documents?
explanation: Preserving all documents is one of the ten ethics, in line with the Bylaw's duty to keep the documents of each transaction.

question: A client wants a sale registered at a lower price than the agreed one and asks the broker to say nothing. May he help?
optionB: Yes, if the gap is small
optionC: Yes, with the other party's consent
explanation: Article 18 bars a broker from facilitating a transaction that violates the laws, and Article 17 requires him to disclose substantial matters honestly.

question: Which act is forbidden by Bylaw No. (85) of 2006?
optionA: Posing as a party without authority
optionB: Giving a party a copy of the file
optionC: Recording each deal in his register
explanation: Article 20 forbids a broker to hold himself out as the second party in a contract he facilitates unless one party authorises it.

question: Who prepares the code of professional ethics that registered brokers must observe?
optionA: The Chamber of Commerce and its board
optionD: The notary public and the courts
explanation: Article 14 says the code of ethics is prepared by the Committee in consultation with qualified and expert real estate brokers.

question: What does the RERA practice guide require brokers to use to record real estate sales?
explanation: The guide says all brokers are mandated to use electronic contracts to record real estate sales transactions.

question: Even when he represents only one party, what must a broker faithfully disclose?
optionA: Only matters the client has approved
optionB: Only the price and the payment dates
optionD: The details and conditions he knows
explanation: Article 19 requires him to disclose the transaction details and conditions he is aware of, even though he represents only one party.

question: In what form must a brokerage agreement be made?
explanation: Article 26 requires a brokerage agreement to be in writing.

question: Which item must a written brokerage agreement state?
optionC: The buyer's bank and loan terms
optionD: The developer's profit on the property
explanation: Article 26 requires the contracting parties' names, the specifications of the real property and the brokerage terms.

question: Where is a brokerage agreement entered under Article 26?
optionA: In the Chamber of Commerce register
optionC: In the Real Property Register record
optionD: On the back of the broker's card
explanation: Article 26 says the brokerage agreement is entered in the record of the Real Property Register.

question: A broker undertakes to find a counterparty and represent the client in negotiation for pay. What is this?
explanation: Article 2 defines a brokerage agreement as one where the broker undertakes to find another party to conclude a contract with the client and represent him in negotiations for remuneration.

question: What is Contract A under the RERA smart contracts?
optionA: A marketing agreement, seller and brokerage
optionB: A sale contract between seller and buyer
optionC: A buyer's purchase wish signed with a broker
optionD: A tenancy renewal form for the unit
explanation: Per the practice guide, Contract A is an agreement to market a property between the seller and the real estate brokerage.

question: What does Contract B record?
optionA: A seller's marketing agreement with the office
optionB: A buyer's wish to purchase, with the broker
optionC: The sale contract between the two parties
optionD: An escrow deposit slip for the project
explanation: Per the guide, Contract B is an agreement of desire to purchase a property between the buyer and the real estate broker.

question: What is Contract F?
optionA: A brokerage contract with the buyer
optionC: An agreement to sell, seller to buyer
optionD: A lease registration form for RERA
explanation: Per the guide, Contract F is the agreement to sell a property between the seller and the buyer.

question: Which contracts must brokers use for marketing and sales, per the RERA guide?
optionA: Templates drawn up by the office
optionC: Notarised letters signed by the owner
optionD: The smart contracts A, B and F
explanation: The guide says RERA provides smart marketing contracts and brokers must commit to using them for real estate marketing and sales.

question: Parties to a Contract F dispute apply for amicable settlement through Trakheesi and fail to agree. What then?
optionA: They go to the judicial authorities
explanation: The guide says that where no amicable solution is reached the parties must resort to the judicial authorities.

question: In an amicable settlement of a Contract F dispute, what does the concerned department do?
optionA: Fines both parties for the breach
optionB: Holds a meeting on the breach
optionD: Reassigns the brokers to new offices
explanation: The guide says the department holds a meeting to discuss the breach and tries to reach an amicable settlement.

question: The parties made no agreement on the broker's fee. How is it fixed?
explanation: Article 27 says remuneration is determined by agreement and, absent agreement, according to prevailing practice.

question: When is a broker entitled to remuneration under Article 28?
optionB: When he introduces a possible client
optionC: When the client signs his agreement
optionD: Only when a contract is concluded
explanation: Article 28 gives the right to remuneration only if a contract is concluded, which is when all parties agree on all conditions in the brokerage agreement.

question: Unless the agreement says otherwise, when does the fee fall due on a sale?
optionA: On signing and registering the sale
optionB: On the first viewing of the unit
optionC: On handover of the keys to the buyer
optionD: One year after the sale is registered
explanation: Article 28(2) gives the broker his remuneration upon signing the sale contract and registering it with the Department, unless the brokerage agreement stipulates otherwise.

question: A sale is conditional on a term agreed in the brokerage agreement. When is the fee due?
optionA: On signing, whether or not it is met
optionC: Never, since the sale is conditional
explanation: Article 28(3) entitles the broker to remuneration only once that term is fulfilled.

question: A brokerage agreement is terminated. May the broker still claim the agreed fee?
optionA: No, termination cancels all fees owed
optionB: Only half of the agreed fee amount
optionC: Yes, absent fraud or gross negligence
optionD: Only after a Council order is issued
explanation: Article 29 keeps his claim to the agreed remuneration except where he is proven to have committed fraud or gross negligence.

question: The broker's efforts fail to produce a contract. May he claim his expenses?
optionA: Yes, in full whenever he asks
optionB: Yes, half of them as compensation
optionC: Yes, if a viewing took place
optionD: Only if the agreement says so
explanation: Article 30 denies compensation or refund of expenses unless the Brokerage Agreement stipulates otherwise.

question: Several brokers worked for one party and the contract was concluded. How is the fee handled?
optionA: Divided as if he were one broker
optionB: Paid to the first one who introduced
optionC: Paid to the biggest firm involved
optionD: Paid in full to each of them
explanation: Article 31 partitions the fee among them as if they were one broker, in line with the terms of the contract they concluded.

question: A seller engaged several brokers separately for one deal. Only one of them closed it. Who is paid?
optionA: All of them, shared out equally
optionB: That broker alone, for the whole fee
optionC: The one the seller chooses later
explanation: Article 32 gives the broker who succeeded in concluding the transaction exclusive entitlement to the whole remuneration.

question: A broker is appointed by both parties. Who pays him?
optionA: The buyer alone pays the whole fee
optionB: The seller alone pays the whole fee
optionC: Each party pays its own share
optionD: The developer pays on both their behalf
explanation: Article 33 makes each party severally liable for his own share even if they agree that one of them will bear the whole.

question: How many persons, with the Department's Legal Advisor, form the Council that settles brokerage disputes?
explanation: Article 34 establishes a Council of four persons and the Legal Advisor, appointed by resolution of the Director General.

question: When will the Council consider a real estate brokerage dispute?
optionA: When the parties agreed so in writing
optionB: Whenever one party files a complaint
optionC: Only after a court has ruled first
optionD: Only when RERA formally refers the case
explanation: Article 35 allows it only where the agreement provides for amicable settlement by the Department or the disputants later agree, in writing, to refer it.

question: What must a written amicable settlement agreement identify?
optionB: The subject matter of the dispute
optionC: The registry value of the unit
explanation: Article 35 requires the subject matter of the dispute to be determined in the amicable settlement agreement document.

question: When may the Council settle a dispute without being bound by the strict rules of law?
optionA: When the broker asks it to relax them
optionB: When the claim is of small value
optionC: When it is authorised to conciliate
optionD: When the developer agrees to it
explanation: Article 36 binds the Council to the rules of law unless it is authorised to conciliate, in which case only rules of public order restrict it.

question: How long does the respondent have to answer an amicable settlement application?
explanation: Article 38 requires the respondent to answer in writing within one week of being notified.

question: Within how long must the Council settle a dispute referred to it?
explanation: Article 38(4) sets a maximum of thirty days from the date of referral of the file, extendable only for valid reasons.

question: Who appoints the secretariat of the brokerage disputes Council?
optionA: A decree issued by the Ruler himself
optionB: A resolution of the Director General
optionC: A vote of the Committee members
explanation: Article 37 says the secretariat is appointed pursuant to a resolution of the Director General.

question: When is a contract deemed concluded for the purposes of the broker's fee?
optionA: When the deposit has been paid in full
optionB: When the viewing of the unit is over
optionC: When all parties agree on all conditions
optionD: When the broker signs the file
explanation: Article 28 deems a contract concluded if all parties agree on all the conditions provided for in the Brokerage Agreement.

question: Which body settles disputes relating to brokerage agreements under Bylaw No. (85) of 2006?
optionB: Dubai Courts as the only forum
explanation: Article 34 sets up a Council at the Department, with jurisdiction to settle disputes relating to brokerage agreements. The Committee handles registration and penalties.

question: In which register are off-plan sales entered?
optionB: The Property Register at handover only
explanation: Law No. (13) of 2008 requires any disposition of a unit sold off-plan to be entered in the Interim Property Register.

question: An off-plan sale is not entered in the Interim Property Register. What is its status?
optionD: Valid if an escrow account exists
explanation: Article 3 makes any sale or other disposition that transfers or restricts ownership of an off-plan unit void unless it is entered in that register.

question: When may a master developer start selling units off-plan?
optionA: On announcing the project to buyers
optionB: After 60% of the units are sold
optionC: After taking the land and approvals
optionD: After the first escrow deposit is made
explanation: Article 4 bars a project or an off-plan sale before the developer has taken possession of the land and obtained the approvals of the competent entities.

question: How does the Department designate a project entered before it is finished?
explanation: Article 4 requires the Department to designate the entry of the real property as under development.

question: Which fees may a developer charge on resale of off-plan or completed units?
optionB: A percentage of the resale price
optionC: Any fee set out in the contract
optionD: A fee agreed with the buyer
explanation: Article 7 forbids any fees on sale, resale or other disposition except administrative costs approved by the Department.

question: When must developers enter a completed project in the Property Register?
optionA: On the first handover to a buyer
optionD: When the defects period has ended
explanation: Article 8 requires completed projects to be entered in the Property Register once the completion certificate is received.

question: A developer wants to market a project through a broker. What must he do under Article 9?
optionA: Contract any licensed agent, keeping it private
optionB: File the contract with the Chamber of Commerce
optionC: Contract a certified broker and register it
optionD: Send a copy to the escrow agent only
explanation: Article 9 of Law No. (13) of 2008 requires a contract with a certified broker under Bylaw No. (85) of 2006, and registration of that contract with the Department.

question: A broker signs a private sale contract for a project not approved by the competent entities. The contract is:
explanation: Article 10 bars developers and brokers from such contracts and makes any contract signed before approval null and void.

question: How much notice does the Department give a purchaser who breaches an off-plan contract before the developer may act (Law No. (9) of 2009)?
explanation: Article 11 as replaced in 2009 requires the Department to give the purchaser thirty days' notice to fulfil his obligations.

question: The purchaser stays in default after notice and the developer has completed at least 80% of the project. What may the developer do?
optionA: Retain only 40% of the unit value
optionB: Retain all payments and claim the balance
optionC: Refund everything and cancel the sale at once
optionD: Retain 25% of the unit value only
explanation: Under Article 11(2)(a) as replaced in 2009, the developer may keep all payments and claim the balance, failing which request a public auction of the property.

question: The developer is at least 60% complete when the purchaser defaults after notice. What is the most the developer may retain on termination?
explanation: Article 11(2)(b) lets the developer terminate and retain a maximum of forty percent of the value of the unit stated in the contract.

question: Construction has started but is below 60%, and the purchaser defaults after notice. The developer may retain at most:
explanation: Article 11(2)(c) lets the developer terminate and retain a maximum of twenty-five percent of the value of the unit.

question: The developer could not start construction for reasons beyond his control, and the purchaser defaults after notice. The developer may retain at most:
explanation: Article 11(2)(d) allows termination with a maximum of thirty percent of the payments the purchaser has made, with no negligence on the developer's side.

question: RERA revokes an off-plan project on a reasoned report. What must the developer do?
optionA: Keep the payments until a relaunch
optionD: Pass the payments to the Department
explanation: Article 11(5) says that where RERA revokes the project the developer returns all payments received, following the procedure in the escrow law.

question: A delivered unit is smaller than the area sold, and the shortfall is not inconsequential. What must the developer do?
optionA: Nothing, the sold area is final
optionB: Cancel the sale and relist it
optionD: Refund the full price in cash
explanation: Article 12 requires compensation for a decrease in area unless it is inconsequential, while an increase gives no right to a higher price.

question: Which register lists the developers licensed to carry on real estate development?
optionC: The Brokers Register kept by RERA
optionD: The Register of Real Estate Developers
explanation: Article 4 of Law No. (8) of 2007 sets up this register, and no developer may operate unless entered in it and licensed.

question: A developer wants to advertise off-plan units in the media. What does Law No. (8) of 2007 require?
optionB: A notice to RERA a month earlier
optionC: A Chamber of Commerce stamp on the ad
optionD: A letter from the master developer
explanation: Article 5 bars advertising or taking part in exhibitions to promote off-plan sales without written authorisation from the Department.

question: In whose name is a real estate development escrow account opened?
explanation: Article 9 of Law No. (8) of 2007 says the account is opened in the name of the project and dedicated exclusively to its construction.

question: May creditors of the developer attach the money in a project's escrow account?
explanation: Article 9 says no attachment may be imposed on the payments deposited in the account for the benefit of the developer's creditors.

question: A developer has three projects under way. How many escrow accounts must there be?
explanation: Article 9 requires a separate Escrow Account for each project.

question: A developer mortgages a project to obtain a loan. Where must the loan amount be deposited?
explanation: Article 13 requires the lending institution to deposit the loan amount in the relevant Escrow Account.

question: After the developer obtains the completion certificate, what share of the escrow account does the Escrow Agent retain?
explanation: Article 14 requires the Escrow Agent to retain five percent of the total value of each Escrow Account.

question: When is the retained part of the escrow account released to the developer?
optionA: On issue of the completion certificate
optionB: Six months after the units are handed over
optionC: One year after units are registered
optionD: After the last instalment is paid
explanation: Article 14 releases the retained amount one year from the registration of units in the names of purchasers.

question: Before marketing an off-plan project, what must the broker ensure, according to the RERA guide?
optionC: The developer is a listed company
optionD: The project is licensed with RERA
explanation: The practice guide requires brokers to ensure licensing and registration of the project, an escrow account tied to it and a marketing contract between developer and brokerage.

question: Where should a buyer of an off-plan unit be told to deposit payments, per the RERA guide?
optionA: Only into the project's escrow account
explanation: The guide tells brokers to instruct buyers to deposit amounts towards properties only in the project's escrow account.

question: How can a broker check that a project is licensed and registered, per the practice guide?
optionA: From the project's printed sales brochure
optionB: Through Mashrooi in the Dubai REST app
optionC: By calling the developer's sales office
optionD: From the master plan shown on site
explanation: The guide says to validate this by logging on to the Dubai REST app and its Mashrooi project service.

question: A purchaser of an off-plan unit may ask the Department to update which entry?
optionC: The registry entry of the plot
explanation: Article 8 of Law No. (8) of 2007 lets a purchaser ask the Department to update the plot's entry to show the purchase agreement with the sub-developer.

question: Do the 80%, 60% and 25% default rules of Article 11 apply to sale contracts for land that is not sold off-plan?
optionA: Yes, they apply to every land sale made
optionB: Yes, but only after one year
optionC: Yes, but in freehold areas only
optionD: No, the parties' own contract governs
explanation: Article 11(6) as replaced in 2009 says its rules do not apply to contracts for land not disposed of by off-plan sale, which follow the terms the parties agreed.

question: Which system issues professional practice cards and office registration certificates?
explanation: The practice guide says Trakheesi handles licences and permits, professional practice cards, office registration certificates and violations and warnings issued to companies.

question: A broker wants to run a classified ad. What must he get first?
optionA: A stamp from the Chamber of Commerce
optionC: A signed Contract B from a buyer
optionD: A copy of the owner's passport
explanation: The guide requires a permit through Trakheesi for any real estate advertisement or marketing material.

question: What must appear on every real estate advertisement?
explanation: The guide says the permit number must be displayed on the ad.

question: Which of these needs a permit through Trakheesi?
optionA: A call to an existing client
optionB: A viewing of a property by appointment
optionC: A written offer to a buyer
optionD: An open day at a property
explanation: The advertisement permit service covers newspaper, SMS, outdoor, vehicle, print, electronic and classified ads, billboards, promotional campaigns and open days.

question: What does the green list let brokers do?
optionA: Call listed owners using their details
optionB: Skip advertising permit rules for open days
optionC: Market projects that have no licence yet
optionD: Waive the escrow account rules for buyers
explanation: The guide says the green list, offered in the Dubai REST app, gives brokers the phone numbers and e-mails of registered owners who are on the list.

question: A broker contacts an owner who is not on the green list. What is the consequence?
optionA: Nothing, if the unit is for sale
optionC: A free renewal of his card
optionD: A permit is issued to him
explanation: The guide says brokers may not contact owners not on the green list, and a violation is issued, with operations suspended on a complaint.

question: Which app holds broker data, the smart contracts and the green list?
explanation: The guide requires all brokers to download the Dubai REST app, which holds broker data, smart contracts, the green list and off-plan project details.

question: What rating should all brokers aim for under the classification standards?
explanation: The guide says RERA classifies offices and brokers by approved standards and brokers should aim for a five-star rating or the golden category.

question: Through which offices are real estate sales registered?
explanation: The guide says sales are handled through registration trustee offices that represent the Land Department in registering sales.

question: Which offices register lease contracts and issue a 'to whom it may concern' certificate?
explanation: The guide says these services go through the real estate services trustee offices that represent the Department.

question: What is the aim of the Dubai Real Estate Brokers Program?
optionD: Auditing the accounts of escrow agents
explanation: The guide says the program trains and qualifies young nationals to take advantage of brokerage job opportunities.

question: Which Owners Association activity does Law No. (16) of 2007 have RERA monitor?
optionA: Setting the prices of the units
optionB: Appointing the managers of each one
explanation: Article 5(8) has RERA monitor and supervise Owners Associations and audit their accounts and records.

question: Which activity besides brokerage does RERA license and regulate?
explanation: Article 5 gives RERA the licensing and regulation of companies engaged in managing real properties and residential compounds.

question: Which does the Land Department itself carry out under Law No. (7) of 2013?
optionA: Hearing rent disputes as a first court
optionC: Licensing banks that lend on property
explanation: Article 6 gives the Department the registration of real property, land surveys and re-surveys and issuing maps.

question: Why are brokerage offices and brokers classified, per the RERA guide?
optionA: To cap the commissions that are charged
optionB: To limit the number of offices open
optionC: To raise competition and service quality
optionD: To fix the prices of every property
explanation: The guide says classification aims at creating healthy competition among brokers and raising the efficiency of services to customers.

question: What may the Committee do with brokers according to Article 44 of Bylaw No. (85) of 2006?
explanation: Article 44 lets the Committee, in consultation with the competent entities, classify brokers according to their specialty and determine the number needed.

question: A balcony measures 20 sqm. Given 1 sqm = 10.764 sqft, what is its area in sqft?
explanation: To convert sqm to sqft multiply: 20 x 10.764 = 215.28 sqft. Dividing instead gives 1.86.

question: A suite has 850 sqft and the service charge is AED 12 per sqft. What is the total service charge?
explanation: Multiply the area by the rate: 850 x 12 = 10,200. Dividing gives 70.83.

question: A 900 sqft unit sits in a building of 45,000 sqft. Annual service fees for the building are AED 360,000. What is this unit's share by area?
explanation: The unit holds 900/45,000 = 2% of the area, and 2% of 360,000 is 7,200, in line with the area-based share in Law No. (27) of 2007.

question: An escrow account's total value is AED 24,000,000. How much does the Escrow Agent retain after the completion certificate?
explanation: Law No. (8) of 2007 keeps 5% of the account's total value: 24,000,000 x 5% = 1,200,000.

question: A unit contract is AED 1,500,000 and the buyer has paid AED 600,000. The project is 85% complete and the buyer stays in default after notice. What balance may the developer claim?
explanation: At 80% or more complete the developer keeps all payments and claims the balance: 1,500,000 - 600,000 = 900,000.

question: A unit contract is AED 2,000,000. The project is 62% complete and the developer terminates after default. What is the most he may retain?
explanation: At 60% or more the cap is 40% of the unit value: 2,000,000 x 40% = 800,000.

question: A unit contract is AED 1,200,000. Construction has started but the project is below 60%. What is the most the developer may retain after default and termination?
explanation: Below 60%, once construction has started, the cap is 25% of the unit value: 1,200,000 x 25% = 300,000.

question: Through no fault of the developer, construction never started. A buyer who paid AED 500,000 defaults after notice. What is the most the developer may retain?
explanation: In this case the cap is 30% of the payments made: 500,000 x 30% = 150,000.

question: A lease has an annual rent of AED 96,000 and no agreed payment dates. How much is each advance instalment?
explanation: The default is four equal instalments paid in advance: 96,000 / 4 = 24,000.

question: Two brokers share a fee of AED 50,000 in the proportion 60:40 under their agreement. What does the 40% broker receive?
explanation: Forty percent of 50,000 is 20,000, and the other broker receives 30,000.

question: A unit measures 1,076.4 sqft. Given 1 sqm = 10.764 sqft, what is its area in sqm?
explanation: To convert sqft to sqm divide: 1,076.4 / 10.764 = 100 sqm.

question: A 1,250 sqft unit sells for AED 2,150,000. What is the price per sqft?
explanation: Divide the price by the area: 2,150,000 / 1,250 = 1,720.

question: In what form must a lease contract be made under Law No. (26) of 2007?
optionA: In writing, signed by both parties
optionD: By a note written by the broker
explanation: Article 4 regulates the landlord-tenant relationship through a written lease contract signed by both parties.

question: What happens to a dispute over a lease that was never registered with RERA?
optionA: It is heard, but a penalty is added
optionB: Courts and government bodies decline it
optionC: Default statutory terms are applied to it
optionD: The broker settles it between them
explanation: Article 4 says judicial authorities and government bodies may not consider a dispute or claim relating to a lease contract unless it is registered with RERA.

question: A lease does not state its term. For how long is it valid?
optionA: For one calendar year in all cases
optionB: For two years as a default term
optionC: For the period set for paying rent
optionD: For the term the landlord chooses
explanation: Article 5 deems it valid for the period specified for payment of the rent where the term is not stated or cannot be proved.

question: The term ends but the tenant stays and the landlord does not object. The lease is renewed:
optionA: Month to month until a notice is given
optionB: For two years on the same terms
optionC: For one year in every case
optionD: For the shorter of old term or one year
explanation: Article 6 renews it for the same term or for one year, whichever is shorter, on the same terms.

question: May either party end a valid lease unilaterally during its term?
optionA: No, only by consent or under the Law
optionC: Yes, after the first six months
optionD: Yes, by the landlord alone, with notice
explanation: Article 7 says a valid lease may not be unilaterally terminated by landlord or tenant, only by mutual consent or under the Law.

question: When does a sub-lease normally expire?
optionD: On the death of the landlord
explanation: Article 8 ends a sub-lease with the main lease unless the landlord expressly agrees to extend it.

question: The parties left the rent unspecified in the lease. What rent applies?
optionB: The landlord's asking rent for the property
optionD: No rent until the parties agree
explanation: Article 9 as amended says that where the parties omit the rent, it is the rent of similar real property, which the Tribunal determines.

question: When no payment dates were agreed, how is the rent paid?
optionA: Monthly, in arrears, in equal parts
optionB: Once, at the end of the lease year
optionC: In two equal instalments, in advance
optionD: In four equal instalments in advance
explanation: Article 12 provides that without agreement the rent is paid annually in four equal instalments, in advance.

question: Unless otherwise agreed, how long before expiry must a party notify the other of a wish to amend terms or not renew?
explanation: Article 14 as amended requires notice not less than ninety days before the lease expires.

question: Unless otherwise agreed, who is responsible for maintenance and repair of defects during the lease?
explanation: Article 16 makes the landlord responsible for maintenance and for repairing any defect that may affect the tenant's intended use.

question: May a landlord alter the property so the tenant can no longer use it fully as intended?
explanation: Article 17 forbids changes that preclude the tenant from full use as intended, and makes the landlord responsible for them.

question: A tenant needs official approvals for decoration works that do not affect the structure. What must the landlord do?
optionA: Refuse the works without a reason
optionB: Charge a fee for each approval
explanation: Article 18 requires the landlord to provide the approvals to the competent entities where the works do not affect the structure.

question: May a tenant change the property or do restoration works on his own initiative?
optionA: No, only with permission and licences
optionB: Yes, minor works need no approval
optionC: Yes, once six months have passed
optionD: Yes, if he restores the unit later
explanation: Article 19 bars changes, restoration or maintenance works unless the landlord permits them and the licences from competent entities are obtained.

question: What may a landlord take from the tenant to cover maintenance at the end of the lease?
explanation: Article 20 allows a security deposit to ensure maintenance, which the landlord must refund, or the remainder, at expiry.

question: How must the tenant return the property at the end of the term?
optionA: Freshly painted in the landlord's colours
explanation: Article 21 requires surrender in the same condition as received, except ordinary wear and tear or damage from causes beyond the tenant's control.

question: Unless agreed otherwise, may a tenant remove leasehold improvements on leaving?
explanation: Article 23 says that unless agreed otherwise the tenant may not remove the improvements he made on vacating.

question: What does a tenant need before sub-letting the property?
optionB: A prior notice filed with RERA
optionC: A letter from the broker involved
explanation: Article 24 says that unless agreed otherwise the tenant may not assign use or sub-let without the landlord's written consent.

question: Within what period after a notice to pay may a landlord seek eviction for unpaid rent?
explanation: Article 25(1) as amended allows eviction where rent is not paid within thirty days of the landlord's notice to pay, unless the parties agree otherwise.

question: Which is a ground to evict a tenant when the lease has expired?
optionA: The tenant requested minor repairs twice
optionB: The rent was once paid a week late
optionC: The owner wants to sell the property
optionD: The tenant brought a pet into the property
explanation: Article 25(2) as amended lists demolition or reconstruction, comprehensive maintenance, the owner's own or a first-degree relative's use, and sale of the leased property.

question: How much notice must a landlord give for an eviction at expiry on those grounds, through a Notary Public or registered post?
explanation: Article 25 as amended requires the Landlord to give the reasons twelve months before the date set for eviction.

question: The Tribunal awards a landlord possession for his own use. How long before he may re-let a residential property to a third party?
explanation: Article 26 as amended bars re-letting before two years for residential property and three years for non-residential property, unless the Tribunal sets a shorter period.

question: After a rebuilt or renovated property is ready, within what time must the former tenant use his right of first refusal?
explanation: Article 29 as amended gives the tenant a right of first refusal, to be exercised within thirty days of the landlord's notice.

question: A landlord cuts off services to the property. What may the tenant do?
optionA: Move out of the property at once
optionB: Wait for RERA to cancel the lease
optionC: Go to the police or the Tribunal
explanation: Article 34 lets the tenant go to the local police station or file a damages claim with the Tribunal, supported by official reports.

question: The landlord of a leased property dies during the term. What happens to the lease?
optionA: It ends on the date of death
optionB: It must be renegotiated in full
optionC: It passes to RERA to manage
explanation: Article 27 says the lease does not expire on the death of the landlord or tenant and continues with the heirs.

question: Which body has exclusive jurisdiction over rent disputes between landlords and tenants in Dubai?
optionB: The Land Department Council of four
explanation: Decree No. (26) of 2013 gives the Centre exclusive jurisdiction over rent disputes in the Emirate and its free zones, with listed exceptions.

question: How long does the Mediation and Conciliation Directorate normally try to reach a settlement from the parties' appearance?
explanation: Article 10 of Decree No. (26) of 2013 sets fifteen days, extendable for the same period by the supervising judge.

question: What is the time limit to appeal a First Instance Division judgment in a rent dispute?
optionA: 7 days from the date of judgment
optionB: 30 days from the date of judgment
optionC: 15 days from the day after hearing
optionD: 60 days from service of the claim
explanation: Article 18 sets fifteen days from the day following the hearing at which the judgment was issued, with a rule for absent defendants.

question: What is the status of a judgment of the Centre's Appellate Division?
explanation: Article 14 makes Appellate Division judgments final and not subject to any form of appeal.

question: When is an Owners Association legally constituted?
optionA: On registering the first unit's sale
optionB: When half of the units are sold
optionC: On issue of the completion certificate
optionD: When a building manager is appointed
explanation: Article 17 constitutes the Owners Association upon registration in the Property Register of the sale of the first unit.

question: Who are the members of an Owners Association?
optionA: Tenants and unit owners together, equally
optionB: Owners, and the developer for unsold units
optionC: Brokers who sold the units, and owners
optionD: Only the master developer, for all the units
explanation: Article 17 says it comprises the owners of units, including the master developer or sub-developer in respect of unsold units.

question: What is the legal nature of an Owners Association?
optionA: A for-profit company owned by the owners
optionB: A branch office of the Land Department
optionC: A non-profit entity with own personality
optionD: An agency of the Dubai government itself
explanation: Article 18 deems it a non-profit entity with legal personality independent of its members, able to sue and be sued in its own name.

question: How are votes at the Owners Association's general assembly allocated?
optionA: One vote per unit, whatever its size
optionB: One vote per owner, however many units
optionC: Equal votes for all the owners
optionD: In proportion to each owner's share
explanation: Article 19 gives each unit owner votes in proportion to his share in the jointly owned property shown in the Master Community Declaration.

question: How is each owner's share of the annual service fees calculated?
optionA: By unit area against total area
optionB: Equally for every unit in the building
optionC: By the purchase price of each unit
optionD: By the rent each unit would fetch
explanation: Article 22 calculates the share from the area of the unit compared to the total area of the jointly owned real property.

question: Who pays the service fees on units that have not been sold?
optionA: The Owners Association from its reserve
optionB: The developer that still owns them
optionC: The Department from its own budget
optionD: Nobody until the units are sold
explanation: Article 22 makes the master developer or sub-developer pay the share of the annual service fees for unsold units.

question: May an owner avoid service fees by waiving his share in the Common Areas?
explanation: Article 22 says a unit owner may not waive his share in the Common Areas to avoid paying his service fees.

question: Which of these is part of the Common Areas unless the Site Plan says otherwise?
optionB: Fixtures that an owner has installed
optionC: Internal doors serving one unit only
explanation: Article 7 lists the structural components, including foundations, columns, structural walls and roofs, as Common Areas.

question: Which of these belongs to the unit rather than the Common Areas?
optionD: The swimming pool of the project
explanation: Article 8 includes fixtures and fittings installed by the owner or occupier in the unit itself.

question: May Common Areas be sold separately from the units they serve?
explanation: Article 16 says Common Areas may not be divided or disposed of, in whole or part, independently of the units to which they pertain.

question: Co-owners of one unit want to divide it among themselves. What is needed?
optionD: Nothing more than the owners' consent
explanation: Article 11 bars sub-dividing a jointly owned unit among its co-owners unless the Department approves.

question: A co-owner offers his share to an outsider. What right do the other co-owners hold?
optionA: A right to veto any outside buyer
optionB: A right to half of the sale price
optionC: A right to block the buyer's financing
optionD: A pre-emptive right to buy it
explanation: Article 12 gives each co-owner a pre-emptive right to buy another co-owner's share offered to a non-owner.

question: The pre-emptive right does not apply when a co-owner's share is sold to:
optionD: A company owned by a friend
explanation: Article 12(2) excludes sales to the spouse, lineal ascendants and descendants, brothers or sisters and their lineal descendants.

question: How long after a Notary notice do co-owners have to agree to the terms before the pre-emptive right expires?
explanation: Article 13 ends the right if the co-owners do not agree to the sale terms within one month of receiving the notice.

question: A co-owner agrees to buy the offered share. Within what time must he notify the seller through the Notary Public?
explanation: Article 13(3) requires notice of intention within fifteen days of receiving the sale notice, then the sale is finalised with the Department within ten working days.

question: A unit owner leases his unit. Who stays bound to the Articles of Association?
optionA: The tenant only, for his stay
optionB: The owner only, until he lets it
optionC: The broker who arranged the lease
explanation: Article 15 says the owner and tenant remain jointly obliged towards other owners and the Association to comply with the Articles and the Master Community Declaration.

question: Unpaid service fees: what security does the Owners Association hold?
optionA: A lien that follows the unit
optionB: A right to sell the unit at once
optionC: A claim against the developer only
optionD: A claim against the tenant only
explanation: Article 25 gives the Association a lien on every unit for unpaid fees, valid even if the title passes to another person.

question: The manager issues a resolution against a defaulting owner. When can it be enforced after notification through a Notary Public?
explanation: Article 25(2) makes the resolution enforceable by the execution judge after three months from notification, with the right to object in court during that period.

question: For how long is the developer liable for structural defects, counted from the completion certificate?
explanation: Article 26(1) keeps the developer liable for ten years from the completion certificate to repair defects in the structural components.

question: For how long is the developer liable for defective mechanical, electrical and plumbing installations?
explanation: Article 26(2) sets one year from the completion certificate for installations such as mechanical and electrical works and sanitary and plumbing installations.
